title: Communication, Connection and Managing Daily Capacity

segments.spoken_text: Welcome back. This session continues the picture we've been building. Sensory experience, thinking and internal signals can all shape communication, connection and the energy available across a day. Keep your own child in mind as we explore these together.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 1; matching slide PDF page 1; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 50; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Let's begin with communication. Before thinking about anyone else's way of communicating, we'll notice how many different ways we already use ourselves.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 2; matching slide PDF page 2; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 51; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Since you woke up today, how have you communicated? Think of three different ways. It could be a spoken greeting, a message, a wave, a look, pointing to something, or taking a moment before responding.

Have a quiet think, then share one example if you'd like to. Pause here for a moment.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 3; matching slide PDF page 3; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 52; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: We all move between different ways of communicating. Speech is one part of that picture. Writing, gesture, a device, showing a photo or moving away can carry a message too. Keep that variety in mind when we consider what helps someone understand and express themselves.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 3; matching slide PDF page 3; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 52; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
The two sides of this slide separate understanding, information coming in, from expressing, messages going out. How much someone speaks doesn't tell us how much they understand. A person may speak fluently and still need support to understand spoken information. Someone else may understand more than they can readily express.

A A C means augmentative and alternative communication. It can include signs, a communication board or book, typing or a communication device. Some people use it alongside speech, and some instead of speech. Communication can change with the setting, the demands and how someone is feeling. Repeated words or familiar scripts can carry meaning too. Stay curious about their purpose and the context.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 4; matching slide PDF page 4; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 53; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: As you watch this video, notice what supports communication. Choose one idea that stands out: perhaps a communication method, something another person does, or something about the environment. Let's hear the speakers' own accounts.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 5; matching slide PDF page 5; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 54; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: What stood out to you about what supported communication? Take a moment to think, or share one observation with someone nearby. Stay close to what the speakers said. Pause here if you'd like longer.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 5; matching slide PDF page 5; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 54; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Keep that observation with you. There is no single Autistic communication profile. We'll now consider the people and places in your child's own communication world.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 5; matching slide PDF page 5; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 54; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to the communication network on page nine. Your child is in the centre. Around them are home, school, friends, community and supports. Add one person or place now. You can write, draw or use a few words.

There is no need to fill every box. A network can be small, changing or still developing. A grandparent, teacher or coach may see different parts of communication. Pause while you add one starting point.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 6; matching slide PDF page 6; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 55; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 9. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: You can return to the rest later, including with your child and other communication partners. This page helps us notice who is connected and what they might need to understand. There is no ranking of who knows your child best.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 6; matching slide PDF page 6; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 55; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 9. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
On the same page, let's think about what useful knowledge could travel between people and places. Purple is a communication strength. Blue is something that helps communication. Orange is something you would like others to know. Use coloured notes if you have them, or the three workbook boxes.

Write one, two or all three. You can use a made-up example, and you can keep your notes private. If you share at a table or on a board, leave out identifying details. Pause now for writing and optional sharing.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 7; matching slide PDF page 7; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 56; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 9. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Look across those ideas. What strengths might be missed if we looked only for speech? Which supports involve changing what a communication partner does or provides? Keep a blue note, or something from the What helps box, in mind. That's our link to the next slide. Useful information can help a child avoid having to start again with every new person.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 7; matching slide PDF page 7; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 56; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 9. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Here are three options to consider alongside what you've written. Clear communication means familiar, specific words and one idea or step at a time. Processing time means allowing space to understand, organise a response and communicate it. Visual supports mean showing information as well as saying it.

The useful support depends on the person and the moment. Try leaving a pause without filling it with more words. Keep the person's communication methods available, including when the message is no. These are ways to make communication more accessible, and we need to check whether they help.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 8; matching slide PDF page 8; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 57; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Visual supports are information you can see and come back to. On this slide, a timer answers how much time is left. A sequence answers what happens next. A daily schedule could answer what is happening today, although that example space is blank in the supplied slide. You might already use a shopping list, calendar or reminder on your phone.

What visual information do you use at home, and what makes it helpful? Share a brief example if you wish, or note one privately. Pause here.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 9; matching slide PDF page 9; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 58; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses. segments.spoken_text: The helpful format differs from person to person. It might be an object, photo, symbol or written words, on paper or a device. Check that the information makes sense and is available when needed. A visual should offer information. Communication tools still need to stay available in their own right.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 9; matching slide PDF page 9; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 58; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses. SOURCE GAP: daily-schedule visual space is blank; narration identifies this and explains the intended format without claiming a missing image is present.

segments.spoken_text:
Connection involves understanding in both directions. The double empathy idea, introduced by Autistic researcher Damian Milton, asks us to consider misunderstandings between people with different experiences and communication styles as a shared gap.

The image shows two people sending and receiving in their own ways. Both have something to understand. You may already do this at home as you learn your child's communication and they learn yours. We can ask what we, as communication partners, might change to make the exchange easier. Listening and adjustment belong on both sides.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 10; matching slide PDF page 10; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 59; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Let's hear one person's experience of being social. As you listen, notice what connection means in this account, without expecting it to describe every Autistic person's experience.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 60; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 60; full speaker notes. segments.spoken_text: Take a quiet moment. What did you notice? You can share one reflection or hold it privately. Pause the video if you need longer.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 60; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Carry that reflection into the next discussion. Connection can take different forms, and the conditions around it can make a difference.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 60; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Social connection can happen in family life, school, the community and online. It may involve conversation, shared interests, doing something alongside another person, quiet company or contact that happens only occasionally. Sharing lots of detail about an interest can itself be a way of reaching towards someone.

Families and cultures also have different ways of being together. Think about the connections your child already enjoys. We can look for what feels meaningful and workable for them, rather than using one style of interaction as the measure for everyone.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 12; matching slide PDF page 12; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 61; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
On page ten, think about when your child seems most comfortable connecting. What do they enjoy: talking, gaming, sport, making something, shared interests, or being together quietly? When does it feel enjoyable, and when does it become tiring or overwhelming?

Then consider what adults could change to make connections safer, easier or more meaningful. Start with your child's preferences. You can reflect privately or talk with your table. Pause for the discussion.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 13; matching slide PDF page 13; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 62; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 10. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: As we return, keep one condition that seems to help in mind. It could be the person, place, activity or amount of time. Some children have few connections right now, and this is not a comparison between families. Meaningful connection can look different across people, settings and days.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 13; matching slide PDF page 13; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 62; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 10. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Now let's look at daily capacity. Something can be enjoyable and still take energy. Communication, sensory processing, transitions and social connection all draw on the resources available in that moment.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 14; matching slide PDF page 14; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 63; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Think of energy as a battery. Each day can begin with a different amount of charge, and activities draw on it. When it runs low, ordinary things can become harder. Many people also use the spoons analogy: a limited supply of energy, with different activities using different amounts.

These are optional ways to describe an experience, rather than measures of ability. The important question is what costs energy and what helps restore it. Rest, familiar interests or a better-fitting environment may help recharge. Support needs to match the charge that is actually available, not the amount we hoped would be there.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 15; matching slide PDF page 15; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 64; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Capacity can vary across a day and from one day to another. Stress, sensory demands, sleep, social situations and other events can change what feels manageable. The same request may be easy on one occasion and too much on another.

Think about what seems to use your child's energy and what lightens the load. We don't need to interpret a change in capacity as unwillingness. It gives us a reason to look again at the demands and the support available.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 16; matching slide PDF page 16; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 65; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Masking can place another demand on energy. We'll hear a first-person account now. Let the speaker describe their own experience, and leave a little room afterwards to reflect.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 17; matching slide PDF page 17; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 66; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 17; matching slide PDF page 17; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 66; full speaker notes. segments.spoken_text: Take a moment before we move on.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 17; matching slide PDF page 17; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 66; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
The image places two moments beside one another: managing at school, and arriving home with very little energy left. Appearing fine may not show the effort underneath.

That doesn't tell us exactly what is happening for every child. It reminds us to consider what a day costs, including effort we may not see. Changes to the environment and expectations can sometimes reduce that effort. We'll return to the after-school experience in our next session.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 18; matching slide PDF page 18; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 67; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
On page ten, consider where your child seems to work hard to appear fine, and where they seem most comfortable being themselves. What could adults change to help them feel more supported?

Start with private thinking. You do not need to prove masking is occurring, or share a personal story. Keep your notes descriptive and your questions open. If you wish, discuss one practical change with your table. Pause here.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 19; matching slide PDF page 19; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 68; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 10. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Keep that possible change in mind. Recognising something now doesn't mean you should have known it earlier. We can learn from new understanding without blame. Making room for a person to be themselves connects directly to the idea on our closing slide.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 3, slide 19; matching slide PDF page 19; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 68; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 10. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Across these two sessions, we've been building a picture of your child. How the world arrives through their senses. How they notice detail, focus deeply and bring particular strengths. How they experience internal signals, communicate and reach towards other people.

Managing those demands every day can take a great deal of energy, especially when the surroundings don't fit. Sensory load, transitions, communication across different styles, and sometimes appearing fine can all add to the cost.

A child who knows who they are, and feels valued for it, has more room for learning, connection and self-understanding. Belonging matters. So does genuine choice about how they communicate, where they feel comfortable and when they need a break. Knowing other Autistic people can offer connection and a sense of shared experience.

Think back to the strengths and joys you wrote down this morning. Supporting a positive Autistic identity can begin with listening, making room for those strengths, and showing that this whole person is worth knowing.

We'll pause here. Take your lunch break when you're ready. When we return, we'll consider what this understanding can look like at home and in the community.
